issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Arthur had managed the Grand Astoria Hotel for twenty-two years, a tenure built on meticulous attention to detail and an unshakeable sense of control. At seventy-six, he still walked the floors with an air of quiet authority, his world a predictable symphony of laundry schedules, reservation systems, and staff briefings. That world shattered six months ago in the hotel's basement. A new cleaning crew had improperly mixed industrial chemicals in the laundry room, creating a toxic chlorine gas that filled the poorly ventilated space. Investigating a strange, acrid smell reported by a housekeeper, Arthur had walked right into the invisible cloud. The memory of it now existed only in shards: the sudden, searing pain in his lungs, a dizzying sense of the concrete floor tilting, and the metallic taste of panic. He couldn't recall how he got out, only the disorienting blur of paramedics and concerned faces.

In the weeks that followed, the inability to piece the event together became a source of profound distress. These fragmented memories, lacking a clear beginning or end, left him with a gnawing conviction that he could no longer trust his own body. A phantom whiff of bleach while walking past the housekeeping carts, an olfactory recall so vivid it made him gasp, would instantly trigger a surge of raw panic. This wasn't a full memory, but an intense, imageless emotion that left his heart hammering against his ribs. The experience cemented a terrifying new belief: he was fundamentally helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to him. This conviction that his body was unreliable and that he was powerless began to transform his world into a landscape of potential danger.

Now, Arthur lives in a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. He feels on guard even within the familiar walls of his own apartment, where every unexpected sound-the hiss of the radiator, a car backfiring on the street below-is processed as an imminent threat. The more on edge he feels, the more the memories seem to break through the fragile barrier he erects around them. A sudden loud noise doesn't just startle him; it can trigger a fragmented sensory recall, a flash of that burning sensation in his throat, which only confirms that he is still in danger. This pervasive sense of threat has deepened his alienation from his own physical self. His body's constant state of alarm feels like a profound betrayal, proof that it has become an enemy that keeps reacting as if the danger is present, even when he knows he is safe.

To cope with this internal chaos, Arthur has developed a rigid set of rules. When the waves of emotion or the phantom smells rise up, his only recourse is to turn the television up until the noise is a physical wall, blocking out the feeling and the fear. This constant sense of being under siege has also dictated his movements. His world has shrunk dramatically; he feels safe only in his living room chair, a tiny island in a sea of perceived threat. At the hotel, the job he once loved has become a minefield. He takes long, inefficient routes to his office to avoid the entire south wing corridor that leads to the basement laundry, the site of the incident. This avoidance, while calming in the moment, serves as a daily confirmation of his own helplessness. Each time he changes his route, it's a silent admission that he cannot handle it, reinforcing the bleak belief that he is no longer in control of his life. At night, he finds himself constantly monitoring his own thoughts, terrified that these strange bodily reactions and memory fragments are the first signs of him "going crazy."

The exhaustion is what finally brought him to seek help. His daughter, visiting for the weekend, was alarmed to find him a prisoner in his own home, with the television blaring and the curtains drawn. Arthur feels trapped in a relentless cycle, his own mind and body the architects of his prison. He is terrified of the memories, but even more so of the belief they have wrought: that he is broken beyond repair. He hopes for a quiet mind and a day where he can trust the simple act of breathing again, but fears that letting his guard down, even for a moment, will invite another catastrophe he won't be able to survive.
